elements.element: Customer has a right to terminate for convenience
elements.evidence: "Customer may terminate this Agreement for convenience"

elements.element: Notice period of 30 days, in writing
elements.evidence: "upon 30 days' prior written notice to Commerce One"

elements.element: Pro-rata refund of prepaid fees on such termination
elements.evidence: "shall refund to Customer any prepaid fees for the period after the effective date of termination"

elements.element: Vendor has no termination-for-convenience right during the committed term
elements.evidence: "Commerce One shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the initial five (5) year term or any renewal term"
clause gives "30 days' prior written notice" (better than fallback, but not the fallback bargain)

elements.element: Early-termination fee not exceeding 3 months' fees
elements.evidence: no early-termination fee is imposed; condition absent

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at end of a term on 90 days' notice
elements.evidence: "shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the initial five (5) year term or any renewal term" (no 90-day end-of-term right granted)

offending_extra_words: For purposes of this Section 11.4, "Customer" means Corio.
reasons: All four preferred atomic elements are present in new Section 11.4: Customer convenience right, 30 days' written notice, refund of prepaid fees for the post-termination period (pro-rata), and an express bar on Commerce One convenience termination during the initial and renewal terms.

The locked preferred level is fully satisfied; no redline of the existing Sections 11.1–11.3 was needed and none was made, so untouched commercial terms (renewal, breach/insolvency termination, survival) remain effective.

Minimality is slightly exceeded: the agreement already uses "Corio" for our party and separately defines "Customer" as Corio's customers, so the added definitional sentence redefining "Customer" for this Section is unnecessary boilerplate — simply naming "Corio" would suffice and would avoid overloading a defined term.
Because the redefinition is expressly scoped "For purposes of this Section 11.4", it does not create an operative contradiction or dangling mechanic elsewhere, so intent is preserved.
